article.title: Bryan Stevenson: America Cannot Repair Racial Injustice Until It Confronts the Lies That Sustain It
article.author: Sharon Kyle
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The Civil War ended slavery, but it did not end the ideas that made slavery possible. That distinction, according to civil rights attorney Bryan Stevenson, helps explain why racial injustice has remained a permanent fixture in American institutions long after the abolition of slavery, the end of Jim Crow, and the victories of the civil rights movement. Speaking with California Governor Gavin Newsom in Montgomery, Alabama, Stevenson offered an analysis of American history that challenges conventional accounts of racial progress. The country's central failure, he argued, has not simply been its unwillingness to acknowledge particular atrocities. It has been its refusal to confront the ideology that justified those atrocities and continues to shape American political life. "I often argue that the north won the Civil War, but the south won the narrative war because those ideas of racial hierarchy prevailed," Stevenson said. That observation captures the central argument of their conversation: Political and legal victories cannot produce lasting racial justice when the beliefs that legitimized oppression remain intact. The Narrative That Survived Emancipation Stevenson, founder of the Equal Justice Initiative, has spent decades challenging wrongful convictions, excessive punishment, racial discrimination, and the treatment of children in America's criminal legal system. His work has convinced him that the most enduring legacy of enslavement was not confined to forced labor or the physical brutality of bondage. "I think the great evil, the enduring evil was the narrative that was created to justify enslavement," he told Newsom. Enslavers needed a moral framework that gave them a justification to continue to regard themselves as decent people even while kidnapping, buying and selling human beings, separating parents from children, and extracting wealth through violence and torture. That framework was the fabricated belief that Black people were inherently inferior to white people. The ideology was essential to the system. Without it, the exploitation of millions of enslaved people would have been much harder to reconcile personally and to reconcile with the nation's professed commitments to liberty, equality, and justice. While it is true that the Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery, except as punishment for crime and the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments promised equal protection and voting rights, those constitutional changes did not eliminate the racial ideology that sustained the institution for generations. With the ideology remaining intact after the abolition of slavery, it simply adapted. After Reconstruction, Southern governments institutionalized racial segregation, disenfranchisement, and racial terror. Courts repeatedly failed to enforce the constitutional protections supposedly guaranteed to formerly enslaved people. The narrative of Black inferiority survived because the nation never undertook the sustained work of dismantling that ideology -- an ideology that exists today. Stevenson sees that failure as a defining feature of American history. The Politics of Fear and Anger The interview took place against the backdrop of renewed political attacks on immigrants, racial minorities, and efforts to teach the history of racism. Stevenson warned that political leaders who mobilize populations through fear and anger are drawing upon a dangerous historical tradition. He cited Nazi Germany and the Rwandan genocide as examples of what can happen when leaders encourage populations to regard identifiable groups as threatening, dangerous, or less than human. In the United States, he sees similar mechanisms operating through narratives that portray marginalized communities as criminal, undeserving, or threatening to the nation's identity. Those narratives can become particularly effective during periods of social and economic uncertainty. Racial resentment offers a political explanation for people's frustrations while directing their anger toward groups that often have relatively little institutional power. Stevenson described racial injustice as a form of inherited pollution. "I've long believed that the history of racial injustice in this country has created these toxins in the air. It's like pollution. We all breathe it in." The metaphor is instructive. Pollution does not require every person breathing contaminated air to have personally created the contamination. Its consequences extend across generations. Likewise, the effects of racial hierarchy persist through institutions, inherited assumptions, public policy, and political language—even among people who reject overt expressions of racial hatred. The danger, Stevenson suggested, is that societies that refuse to acknowledge these influences remain susceptible to leaders who know how to exploit them. Why Truth Must Come Before Repair Newsom's conversation with Stevenson also addressed reparations and the responsibilities of institutions that profited from enslavement and subsequent racial discrimination. In introducing the episode, Newsom described signing legislation requiring certain longstanding corporations to examine and publicly disclose historical connections to slavery. The examples included insurance policies written on enslaved people and financial transactions in which human beings were treated as collateral. Stevenson argued that meaningful repair requires an honest accounting of the harms committed. For him, truth-telling, accountability, reconciliation, and reparations are related but distinct stages of a larger process. "You've got to commit to truth-telling before you get to the beautiful R word," he explained. This is more than a moral appeal. Institutions cannot meaningfully repair harms they have not identified. Governments cannot design remedies without examining how past policies distributed wealth, opportunity, political power, and disadvantage. And the public cannot evaluate proposals for reparations without understanding what was taken, who benefited, and how those benefits and losses continue to shape the present. Stevenson pointed out that American society readily accepts financial compensation when contracts are violated or property rights are infringed. Yet demands for reparations following centuries of racial exploitation are frequently treated as unreasonable or divisive. The contrast reveals how differently the nation values injuries to property and injuries to human dignity. Repair, in this understanding, is not simply a matter of writing checks. It requires confronting the institutions and economic arrangements through which racial inequality was created and maintained. Remembering the History America Tried to Forget The setting for the conversation was particularly significant. Montgomery is home to the Equal Justice Initiative's Legacy Museum and National Memorial for Peace and Justice, which opened in 2018. These institutions document the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans, American enslavement, racial terror lynchings, segregation, and the connections between that history and mass incarceration. Stevenson described their purpose as filling a fundamental gap in American public memory. He compared the United States' treatment of its racial history with Germany's efforts to confront the Holocaust. German memorials, museums, educational requirements, and public markers make Nazi atrocities difficult to ignore. The United States, by contrast, has historically dedicated far more public space to celebrating powerful political and military figures than to remembering people who suffered under racial domination. Stevenson's point is not that remembering atrocities automatically prevents their recurrence. It is that deliberate public remembrance creates opportunities for education, acknowledgment, and accountability that collective silence cannot provide. His work in Montgomery demonstrates that confronting history need not remain an abstract intellectual exercise. Museums, memorials, historical markers, and documented personal stories can transform public understanding of events that have too often been omitted or misrepresented. The project also challenges communities beyond the South to recognize their own connections to racial exploitation. Enslavement was not exclusively a Southern institution. Northern ports, banks, insurance companies, and commercial enterprises also participated in and benefited from the economy of human bondage. A truthful national history must account for those connections. From Racial Terror to Mass Incarceration One of Stevenson's most consequential arguments concerns the connection between racial hierarchy and the American criminal legal system. The ideology that portrayed Black people as inherently inferior eventually evolved into narratives depicting them as inherently dangerous. Those narratives helped legitimize racial terror lynchings, discriminatory policing, harsh criminal sentencing, and policies that contributed to mass incarceration. Stevenson described the experience of representing clients who should have enjoyed the presumption of innocence but were instead presumed dangerous or guilty because of their race or poverty. He also recalled being threatened at gunpoint by police officers despite having graduated from Harvard Law School. His professional achievements did not insulate him from racial suspicion. The experience illustrates the limitations of approaches to racial inequality that emphasize individual educational attainment or economic advancement while neglecting systemic discrimination. Stevenson's broader point is that a society cannot understand mass incarceration without confronting the historical narratives that made extraordinary levels of punishment politically acceptable. During the late twentieth century, descriptions of young people as "super predators" helped justify increasingly punitive policies, including severe sentences imposed on children. Stevenson and the Equal Justice Initiative subsequently challenged such practices, securing major Supreme Court victories against mandatory life-without-parole sentences for children. He continues to question the moral legitimacy of the death penalty in a criminal legal system marked by racial discrimination, wrongful convictions, and unequal access to effective legal representation. For Stevenson, the central question about capital punishment is not simply whether a person convicted of a terrible crime deserves to die. It is whether a government operating through a profoundly imperfect system should exercise the power to kill. Hope Is Not the Same as Optimism Despite the weight of the history he described, Stevenson repeatedly returned to the necessity of hope. Newsom pressed him on how Americans should maintain hope amid political exhaustion, polarization, historical revisionism, and the continuing erosion of democratic norms. Stevenson's answer rejected the idea that hope depends on expecting circumstances to improve on their own. Hope is a discipline that creates obligations. He described an enslaved great-grandfather who risked punishment to learn to read and write when doing so was prohibited. After emancipation, that ancestor read newspapers aloud to formerly enslaved neighbors who had been denied literacy. Stevenson's grandmother inherited that commitment to education, eventually passing it to her children and grandchildren. Although she worked as a domestic worker throughout her life, she insisted that education could open possibilities for future generations. Stevenson remembered that his mother purchased a set of encyclopedias for the family even though doing so required taking on debt. He had never met a lawyer before attending Harvard Law School. Yet his family's insistence on learning helped make that future imaginable. Those experiences shaped his conviction that people have a responsibility to continue struggles whose outcomes they may never personally witness. "I just think it's what we owe our children. It's what we owe the future," he said. The distinction matters. Optimism can become an expectation that progress is inevitable. Hope, as Stevenson describes it, demands action even when progress appears uncertain. It is the conviction that people must struggle for a more just society because the alternative is to surrender that society's future to those most willing to exploit fear and division. The Work of Changing the American Story Perhaps the most important lesson of the conversation is that changing laws without changing public consciousness leaves the foundations of injustice vulnerable to reconstruction. Stevenson pointed to changes in public attitudes toward smoking and drunk driving as examples of how new information, sustained advocacy, and powerful personal narratives can transform social behavior and eventually public policy. He believes a similar transformation is necessary in America's understanding of racial injustice. "Learning is an action item," he insisted. But learning must be followed by participation. His emphasis on proximity—the importance of bringing people closer to the experiences of those who are marginalized—challenges the political and social arrangements that allow privilege to remain insulated from suffering. It also offers a response to the temptation to withdraw from civic engagement when conditions become overwhelming. At the conclusion of the conversation, Stevenson recalled a particularly difficult moment after an unsuccessful resentencing hearing for a client who had originally received life without parole as a child. Exhausted and discouraged, he stopped at a restaurant. A group of older Black women recognized him. One called him over, instructed him to bend down, kissed him on the forehead, and offered a simple instruction: "You keep on keeping on." The encounter reminded him that movements for justice are sustained not only by landmark court decisions and prominent leaders, but by ordinary people who recognize the importance of the struggle and encourage those carrying it forward. That understanding connects Stevenson's personal history with his institutional work and political analysis. The struggle for racial justice is also a struggle over what Americans are willing to remember, what they are prepared to acknowledge, and what kind of future they believe they have an obligation to create. The Civil War ended the legal institution of slavery. The civil rights movement dismantled much of the formal architecture of Jim Crow. But neither achievement fully defeated the narrative of racial hierarchy. Stevenson's message is that the next stage of American democracy must confront that unfinished work. Truth must become a public responsibility. Accountability must extend to institutions that benefited from racial exploitation. Repair must address the consequences of historical injustice. And hope must be translated into sustained collective action. Without those commitments, the nation risks continuing a familiar pattern: condemning the most visible manifestations of racial oppression while preserving the conditions that allow them to return in new forms. America's future, Stevenson suggests, depends on whether the country can finally replace the lies that justified racial domination with a more truthful understanding of its history—and a more expansive commitment to justice.
